title: In search of more Christmas films like It's a Wonderful Life

commenti.body:
1951’s Scrooge is the other best Christmas film I can think of; obviously there are many (inverse) parallels to It’s a Wonderful Life.

The Green Knight (2021) may not be thought of as a Christmas film but I’d say it really is—less so than the poem though.

I’m sure there are lots of fantastic older ones if you want the focus on family as the true meaning of Christmas, though I haven’t seen them myself.
Thank you, not even family necessarily but also themes of like no matter how much suffering you're enduring know that life is worth it for the likes of what Christmas is for. If that makes sense?

I’d say there’s a reason It’s a Wonderful Life is such a classic and one of my top few favorite films. 

A Christmas Carol is similar in that it actual has meaning etc but I’m not a huge fan of any of the film versions, have always found the stage plays to be much better. 

I think The Holdovers is based around Christmastime and while I’ve not seen it yet, everything I’ve heard has been very positive.
[removed]

My favorite Christmas film is The Long Kiss Goodnight. Going on the journey of the lead character to discover her identity is just so thrilling! She battles with whether or not she loves her family as she discovers who she really used to be. It’s also at times super campy. I don’t want to ruin the plot. But the Christmas time journey the lead character goes through is exciting.

Sooooo many awesome Christmas movies from the 1940s. Being made during wartime and postwar times, the caring for one’s fellow man predominates in nearly all themes, and does so with a lightness and humorous touch. 

As for The Holdiovers, it’s very good, but time will tell if it has any replayability.
[removed]

Not a Christmas movie but A Matter of Life and Death has a similar feel and theme. 

Adding some nonsense to get to the required characters. Nice weather we are having for this time of year. I remember it was much colder this time last year.

Tokyo Godfathers! I saw it in theaters a few days ago and can't recommend it enough. It's about reconnecting with family (and finding family in the community around you), miracles/coincidences, and how hope can come from anywhere and anybody. It can get a bit heavy, but has plenty of levity and a very positive message. The heart and humanity this film shows moved me in a way that few other movies have.

"It Happened on 5th Avenue" (1947).  

Takes place during the depression and made commentary on homelessness and generosity.  It's  more comedy oriented than "Its a Wonderful Life" but has a message in a similar vein.  I personally prefer it, and it's one of my all-time favorite Christmas movies.
Seconded, this is an excellent film.
It’s too much of a slog to be repeatable. It’s good, but pacing is slow.

I ve become and big champion for Holiday Affair (1949) it’s a great rom-com with a young Janet Leigh as a war widow mum who accidentally gets Robert Mitchum fired from his retail job just before Christmas. Sparks fly and she must choose between free spirit Mitchum and boring but dependable Wendell Corey. The child actor who plays Leigh’s kid is a total charmer too.

Although it isn't explicitly a Christmas movie, Greta Gerwig's Little Women (2019) has entered my regular Christmas movie canon because it understands and exemplifies those same ideas you're looking for. 

Plus there are Christmas scenes in the movie so it's not *not* a Christmas movie.
Highly subjective take. Gentle slow movies have loads of replayability for me if the vibe works.
Saw it not long ago and it still holds up! Another great one is Remember the Night! and The Man who Came to dinner
[removed]
They are both great, especially Remember the Night, I adore Stanwyck
[removed]

Remember the Night, Holiday Affair and Bishop's Wife have a very similar vibe.

In general, the 40s had a lot of classic Christmas films that still hold up well (and don't feel as cynical as some of the modern Christmas movies).

There’s a great short film called The Christmas Star. I forget what year it is, but I believe it’s the 1940’s. Last I checked it was on YT. Similar vibes to Its a Wonderful Life.

It’s got a cynic who realizes he’s wrong about humanity’s inherent good nature played against an allegory of the holy family without being explicitly religious.

While it’s technically not a Christmas film, The Miracle of Morgan’s Creek is a spectacular film that satirizes the biblical Christmas narrative and the U.S.’s ongoing involvement in the Second World War. Sturges is a genius filmmaker and the story of how he fought censor boards to make the film is amazing.

Holiday Affair (1949) shows that Mitchum can do romance and not just dramatic, being the antagonist or villain. He's such a great actor, so much range. This is definitely a movie that many people just don't know exists.
[removed]
I wouldn't say it has a christmas vibe, but it's a terrific film. One of Sturge's best for sure!

The Shop Around The Corner (1940) absolutely hits that spot. It’s a classic. Ernst Lubitsch at the top of his game. It also inspired You’ve Got Mail.

You also can’t go wrong with Minnelli’s Meet Me In St. Louis.

But, for a deeper recommendation, Bergman’s Fanny And Alexander is simply sublime.  It’s a masterpiece.  It’s long though.  Preferred version is the 5 hour miniseries which you can watch as 1 hour episodes.

Funny enough Howard Hughes was the one who insisted Mitchum played the romantic role in this one. It was essentially a PR move to show him as a nice guy, after his brief conviction for Marijuana possession.

Since the movie was a commercial flop, the move didn't really work. However the conviction didn't really affect his career anyway.
She's also in Christmas in Connecticut, another holiday classic.
I'll die on the hill that the best christmas carol version is the 70s musical directed by Ronald Neame and starring Albert Finney.
[removed]
Fanny and Alexander is truly a christmas classic, even though it's mostly only during the first hour or so..
I second this, it’s been in my Christmas rotation since it released.
The 1994 one, too! I love them both.

Stubby Pringle’s Christmas (1978). It’s a western Hallmark movie starring Beau Bridges and genuinely delightful. It used to air on TV, but they lost the rights due to issues with the author’s estate and it never got an official release. My dad taped over my mom’s copy and spent like 15 years trying to track down another. There are low-quality rips available on YouTube. I might be biased due to it being a white whale in my family for so long, but I think it’s a masterpiece.
Muppets Christmas Carol is a ton of fun!

There's the other Jimmy Stewart Christmas movie, The Shop Around the Corner. While this is mostly a romance, what I found most compelling was the subplot of the rich boss who is having a really hard time in his personal life making a much-needed friend in the young delivery boy, who is an orphan living in a boarding house.
Holdovers is indeed great! I should say though that it’s not really a “true meaning of Christmas” type of movie. It’s more christmassy than, say, Die hard, but not any more than, say, Home Alone.

Okay, so I’ve got a real hipster deep cut for you that I think is kinda perfect, but also slightly off topic. The director of The Bicycle Thieves, Vittorio de Sica directed this really lovely, warm-hearted movie called “Miracle in Milan”. I believe it technically isn’t a Christmas movie, but my old Italian film teacher claimed that it was considered a sort of classic Christmas watch in Italy. I think there’s a sort of parable-istic tone to it, and if I recall, some minor magical realism. So in those ways it might be more in line with what you’re aiming for than a lot of literal Christmas movies. (It’s also possible I’m forgetting and it actually *is* set during Christmas!)
[removed]
[removed]
And weirdly one of the more faithful adaptations of the charles dickens novella.
[removed]
De Sica is hipster now?
[removed]
I watch that first part every Christmas Eve
A great movie

Dude!!! such an under rated Christmas movie, not a Christmas movie as such but based in around the time of the holiday season, great movie, love the story, some cheesy moments for sure but whatever, found the narrative towards the end intriguing....
[removed]

Family Man with Nicholas Cage. A very very under rated feel good Christmas movie, more of a modern movie as opposed to an oldie, it always seems to fly under the radar for some reason.

It's about a very rich business man who at one point leaves the love of his life to follow his career. Years later his life gets turned upside down when an angel gives him a glimpse of what his life could have been like had he not chosen his career instead of the woman he was once in love with. 

Sounds cheesy, because it is a bit, but it's still a good Christmas movie none the less.
[removed]

Like many other people I have a great suggestion that’s not technically a Christmas movie. Riders Of Justice begins with a man buying a Christmas gift for his granddaughter and ends on Christmas Day. A lot of shit goes down in between though. This is a Christmas movie more like Die Hard than it’s a wonderful life, but it’s also nothing like die hard or any American action movie. It’s hard to say what kind of movie it is, there’s comedy, intense action, and some of incredibly moving dramatic. moments, and it’s taking place during Christmas. It features at least two (Mads Mikkelson is just incrédible). 

I guess it came to mind because like it’s a wonderful life, it ends on Christmas and it’s one of the best movies I’ve ever seen.

Kind of a downer but "A Midnight Clear" is one I try to watch every year. 

Takes place in WWII, early in the Battle of the Bulge, American & Germans work some things out for Christmas but then.....
This is what immediately comes to mind for me. He doesn't go Full Cage, but his acting is very good.
Hahaha yeah he doesn't go 'full cage' (love that expression), it has a bit of everything, mostly comedy but he plays the part well I have to say
Shop Around The Corner is SO FKN GOOD.
[removed]

Miracle on 34th Street (1947) is on my Christmas rotation for similar reasons to It's a Wonderful Life. Very different tone, but Joyeau Noel (2005) is another very compelling Christmas film based on a true story during WW1.

My wife loves this movie and watches it every Christmas. At first I thought it was... I don't know, I couldn't put my finger on it, but I thought it was good Cage. Now, after having watched every Christmas the last ten years, I love it, and agree it is underrated, misunderstood, and a modern classic

The self-conscious “hipster” comment was not in relation to De Sica, but rather to myself in being like “nah, guys, the REAL good stuff is not American movies, but deep-cut 1950s foreign language films!” 

I can imagine people seeing that and quite reasonably thinking I’m trying to peacock with an obscure foreign title.

I mean, a black and white Xmas movie with suicide attempts, anti-capitalist sentiment, and a dude being totally played by those around him is a toss up between It’s a Wonderful Life and The Apartment.
[removed]
[removed]

When I'm feeling snarky, I go for Terry Zweigoff's Bad Santa or Alex de la Iglesias' El Dia de Bestia.  When I'm not, I'll go for It's a Wonderful Life, or Joyeux Noël (2005), which is about the spontaneous WW1 Christmas Armistice of 1914.  It gets me every time.

Capras last film Pocketful of Miracles maybe up your alley a little long in the tooth but fantastic performances. 

Also a little mawkish and broad but '29th street' is very much in the vein of Its A Wonderful Life 

Tokyo Godfathers also good!
Well, I'm still puzzled you think Miracle in Milan is an obscure film. It's a critically acclaimed neo-realist film, even though it's a fairy tale.
Pocketful of Miracles is alright, but it's a remake of 'Lady for a Day', also by Capra which is the superior version. I'd reccomended checking that one out
[removed]
[removed]
[removed]
It's also a bit depressing, it's a great story, but Idk if I'll come back to The Holdovers every holiday season.

I've always loved A Christmas Carol (1951). It feels a little dry at first, but once Jacob Marley shows up it really takes you on the journey. Everything about this movie feels so old, the 1800s London sets are very believable. The scenes of desolation, where Scrooge is alone or screaming in despair amid some dusty parlor room, make it so that the joyful scenes (Fezziwick's and Fred's parties) really pop. Alistair Sims sells the old curmudgeon so thoroughly that his transformation hits like a ton of bricks at the end.

Completely different style and tone but Satoshi Kon's Tokyo Godfathers is an absolute gem of a Christmas film. It deals extensively with very real issues like homelessness, mental health, loss of family. But it still manages to be utterly charming and a hell of a lot of fun.
Had to go all the way to the bottom of this thread to find my pick! Great rec.
[removed]

One favorite I haven't seen mentioned yet is *The Cheaters*, also known as *The Castaway* from 1945. Starring Joseph Schildkraut (*The Shop around the Corner*, *The Life of Emile Zola*), Billie Burke (Glinda from *The Wizard of Oz*), and Eugene Pallette (*My Man Godfrey*), it's a slightly silly but effective Christmas story that pits a scheming and opportunistic upper class family against their own conscience, with Schildkraut and some Christmas schmaltz supporting the latter's cause. It's worth seeking out (I believe both YouTube and archive.org have copies) for any classic Christmas film enthusiast.
klaus. really beautifully animated film that tries a new take on santa's origin. definitely fits what you're looking for and isn't as reductive as you would expect from an animated christmas film.
Just watched this again. I always feel bad for Wendell Corey. He’s a good guy and doesn’t deserve how he gets treated.

By far my favorite version. 

If you look closely at the scene where he wakes up Christmas morning and looks in the mirror, you can see the reflection of the camera operator. 

Also, there’s a really lovely little moment when he goes to Fred’s and hesitates before going in, not sure he’ll be welcomed after his previous behavior. He looks questioningly at the maid who answers the door, who gives him the tiniest little nod, the permission he needs to join the party, to reconnect with his only family and society in general. Not a word is spoken, she’s a character who only exists in those few seconds, but somehow the whole third act is contained in those few gestures.

John Ford’s Three Godfathers from 1948. At Christmas time three outlaws pursued by a posse find a dying woman and her newborn baby and promise to bring the child through the desert to the town of New Jerusalem. Just lovely.
Very true
Shop around the Corner is ok but it's not Lubitsch at the top of his game...

I absolutely love The Family Man!  It feels so hopeful and optimistic to me more so than Its a wondeful life.  Even though nick cages character is in midlife he has so much potential to achieve the life his is shown.  Its a wonderful life kinda makes me sad as someone who feels some regret about settling down so young.  I realize after being shown his glimpse George recognizes how much he took his life for granted.  But I feel we cant choose our dreams and I feel sad that it appears George may never realize his dreams of traveling the world.  Mary gets her dream but George might not ever get his, It feels unfair.

*It's a Wonderful Life* might be my favorite movie period, not just Christmas movie (*Lion In Winter*, *Casablanca*, *LA Confidential* are the other contenders, depending on my mood);  *Die Hard*'s probably my favorite festive Christmas movie
Oh neat! Wasn’t the store Meg Ryan owned in You’ve Got Mail called “The shop around the corner “?

The Green Knight is a fantastic choice, phenomenal movie and it totally is a Christmas movie imo.
